MR. DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: Mr. Jethmalani, the debate is over. Do you want to 
say something? 
SHRI RAM JETHMALANI (Maharashtra): Sir, I just want to say one 
thing. First of all, merely because an order under section 144 is in operation and 
somebody comes and makes a breach of that order is not a justification for a 
lathicharge. Alathicharge can only be resorted to if those people, by their 
conduct, are endangering the safety of the police, the police find no other 
method of safeguarding themselves and safeguarding themselves from hurt and 
injury, and they used reasonable force fo r retaliation. Now, this is the law. 
Therefore, what is of importance in these matters is: Who are the aggressors 
first? Merely because section 144 is there, people can say, "Well, we are 
committing a breach of your 144, please prosecute us". You are only entitled to 
arrest them, take them to a police station and ultimately prosecute them in a court 
of law. Today, what is important is: What is the first immediate version coming 
from the Government side as to the circumstance under which this lathicharge 
started? The police, unfortunately, in this country has unlimited capacity to 
fabricate false evidence. Today the House should know what the immediate 
version is. What was it that led the police to lathicharge? What was the danger 
that they apprehended to their life and liberty? Why was it necessary to use this 
kind of force? 
Sir, I only wish to say this. I don't wish to prejudge any issue. But looking 
at the television and looking at the newspaper pictures, it does appear to me 
prima facie, at least, a case of unbridled, limitless and avoidable brutality. 
SHRI SHIVRAJ V. PATIL: I have been very careful. I have received the 
version given by the State Government. We have also heard the hon. Members 
who spoke here. In the other House, one of the hon. Members who had gone to 
the spot and met the people there, has also given his version. I think two hon. 
Members of this House also had gone there. There is a contradiction between 
the two statements which have been received by us. So I have tried to avoid the 
contradiction. Why have I tried

Statement-I 
Copy of the Joint Press Statement issued by Ministry of Petroleum in 
India and Pakistan 
In accordance with the Joint Press Statement of April 18,2005, in New Delhi 
by the President of Pakistan, His Excellency General Pervez Musharraf and 
the Prime Minister of India, His Excellency Mr. Manmohan Singh, it was agreed 
that the Ministers of Petroleum and Natural Gas would meet to explore 
cooperation on the issue of pipelines. Accordingly, the Indian minister for 
Petroleum & Natural Gas and Panchayati Raj, Shri Mani Shankar Aiyar, visited 
Pakistan at the invitation of H.E. Mr. Amanullah Khan Jadoon, Minister for 
Petroleum and Natural Resources of Pakistan, between June 5-7, 2005. The two 
Ministers discussed cooperation between India and Pakistan with regard to the 
import of gas through transnational pipelines. 
2. In Islamabad, H.E. Mr. Mani Shankar Aiyar had the honour of calling on 
H.E. President General Pervez Musharraf and H.E. Prime Minister Mr. Shaukat 
Aziz. He had a one-to-one meeting and delegation-level talks with H.E. 
Minister Mr. Amanullah Khan Jadoon. The two Ministers agreed that the 
transnational pipeline projects should be given top priority as there would be 
substantial advantage to both countries in pursuing and realizing cooperation 
in these projects, to serve their energy security interests, and to create linkages 
and inter-dependencies for establishing an enduring relationship between the two 
countries. They were of the shared view that, given the substantial requirements of 
gas of their countries, the processing of pipeline projects should be accelerated. 
3. The Indian Minister explained to the Pakistani Minister India's 
requirements of gas by pipeline and the arrangements worked out by India. The 
Pakistan side gave a detailed presentation of the position regarding supply and 
demand for natural gas in Pakistan and provided an overview of the gas sector 
economy. The' Indian Minister thanked the Pakistani side for the detailed 
information provided and, in turn, provided some details of arrangements made by 
India to import LNG and agreed to share technical inforamtion and experience in 
this regard with the Pakistani side. 
49 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2005] 
4. Iran-Pakistan-India Pipeline: The two Ministers reviewed the Iran-Pakistan-India 
gas piepline proposal. They agreed that the project, which envisaged supply of gas to 
Pakistan and India through a transnational pipeline, would go a long way in meeting the 
energy security requirements of the two countries and, thus, should be seen as a significant 
project for the benefit of the people of these countries. The Indian and Pakistani 
delegations agreed to exchange information in regard to the financial structuring, 
technical, commercial, legal and related issues to realize a safe and secure world class 
project. To this end, it was agreed that the momentum pertaining to the project should be 
accelerated by constituting a Joint Working Group at the Secretary-level, which will meet 
regularly and report progress to the Ministers to facilitate definitive decisions by them, 
at the earliest. 
5. Turkmenistan-Afghanistan-Pakistan Pipeline: H.E. Mr. Amanullah Khan Jadoon 
provided the Indian Minister with details of this project in which the Indian side 
expressed interest. The Indian Minister confirmed that he would respond positively to an 
invitation to attend the next Steering Committee Meeting. 
6. Gulf South Asia (GUSA) Pipeline: The Pakistani side outlined the parameters of 
the proposed GUSA project and India expressed interest in participating in this project. 
7. The Indian Minister conveyed his gratitude to H.E. Mr. Amanullah Khan Jadoon 
for the warm hospitality and courtesy extended to him and his delegation throughout their 
stay in Pakistan. Minister Aiyar invited Minister Amanullah Khan Jadoon to visit India to 
pursue transnational pipeline projects to maintain the momentum of dialogue and 
cooperation. The invitation was accepted. It was decided that H.E. the Pakistani 
Minister would visit India at his earliest convenience. It was also agreed that the Indian 
Minister would again visit Pakistan at mutual convenience later in the year. These visits 
would be preceded by meetings of the Joint Working Group, alternately in India and 
Pakistan, to discuss all issues relevant to the realization of world-class pipeline projects to 
meet the gas requirements of the two countries.

Copy of the Joint Press Statement issued by India and Pakistan 
The first meeting of the India-Pakistan Joint Working Group (JWG) on 
cooperation in transnational pipelines was held in New Delhi on 12th - 13th 
July, 2005. The Indian delegation was led by Shri S.C. Tripathi, Secretary, 
Ministry of Petroleum & Natural Gas, while the Pakistani delegation was led 
by H.E. Mr. Ahmad Waqar, Secretary, Ministry of Petroleum and Natural 
Resources. Besides having substantial delegation level discussions, the Pakistani 
delegation called on H.E. Shri Mani Shankar Aiyar, Indian Minister of Petroleum 
& Natural Gas and Panchayati Raj, who conveyed the firm support of the 
Government of India to the Iran-Pakistan-mdia Piepline Project and other 
transnational pipeline proposals under consideration. He urged the two delegations 
to prepare a time frame in respect of various items pertaining to the project. 
2. The discussions between the two delegtions were marked by a positive 
and constructive approach and were held in an atmosphere of candour and 
mutual understanding. Both sides conveyed their serious commitment to 
address various issues pertaining to the project so as to maintain the momentum 
of the dialogue. They agreed that dialogue on the basis of bilateral joint working 
groups between India, Pakistan and Iran, interspersed with periodic 
interactions at Ministerial level, provided a satisfactory mechanism to address 
and resolve all matters pertaining to the project. 
3.The two delegations had an indepth discussion of the technical, financial, 
commercial and legal aspects of the project. The two sides agreed that in order to 
realize a safe and secure world class project, arrangements would need to be 
provided for in every as pect of the project, including technical, commercial, 
financial and legal matters 
4. The two sides agreed that once basic issues pertaining to the project had 
been satisfactorily resolved between the three countries concerned, they would 
enter into a "Framework Agreement." In this regard, it was agreed that the 
Indian side would submit a draft text to the Pakistani side before the next 
meeting of the JWG. 
5. The two sides agreed that they shared an immediate commonality of interest 
in regard to the technical aspects of  the project such as the size and 
specifications of the pipeline, the quality of gas, the quantum of gas

these would be established on the basis of techno -economic considerations. 
7. The two sides agreed that the price of the gas as well as the project structure were of

latest developments pertaining to the project as also on their recent discussions pertaining 
to the GUSA Project.

SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) Given the in creasing gap between demand and 
domestic availability of cr ude oil, besides taking measures to accelerate 
exploratory activities for enhancing domestic oil and gas production, it has

enriched uranium, much of which is and will continue to be imported, India has

thorium for electricity generation, Department of Atomic Energy is pursuing a 
three-stage nuclear power programme. The three stages of the programme have 
to be gone through sequentially. The first stage has reached a status of 
commercial maturity. There are 15 nuclear power reactors totaling a capacity

The third stage of the programme will be launched once we have reached a 
sizeable capacity in the second stage. 
The estimated potential of renewable energy such as wind, small hydro and 
bio-mass is about 80,000 MW in the country. The aim is to deploy ar ound 
3,000 MW capacity from renewables durign the 10th Plan period, comprising

*34. SHRI T.T.V. DHINAKARAN:  Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that salinisation of sub-soil water is taking 
place in the coastal region and even in interior areas; 
(b) whether Government have assessed the impact of this salinisation of sub-
soil water in the country; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) the steps taken/proposed to be taken by Government to protect sub-soil 
water? 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (SHRI PRIYARANJAN 
DASMUNSI): (a) to (d) Studies carried out by the Central Ground Water Board 
(CGWB) and the State Ground Water Departments have indicated salinisation of 
ground water in some parts of the States of Andhra Pradesh, Goa, Gujarat, 
Karnataka, Maharashtra, Orissa, Tamil Nadu, West Bengal and Union Teritory 
of Pondicherry. 
Details of State-wise impact of this salinisation is as follows:— 
Andhra Pradesh: Salinity in ground water has been noticed in parts 
of coastal districts fo East Godavari, West Godavari, Prakasam, 
Visakhapatnam, Gunturand Krishna. Sa linity in these areas has its 
genesis to the inherent marine deposition and is not due to sea water 
intrustion. 
Goa: Low lying estuarine regions of various west flowing rivers in the 
State are affected by salinity ingress due to tidal inflow. 
Gujarat: Due to progressive sea water intrusion, the quality of 
ground water is steadily deteriorating in coastal tracts of Kachchh and 
Saurashtra. 
Karnataka: Three districts viz. Uttara Kannanda, Udupi and 
Dakshina Kannada are affected by the problem of salinity ingress in 
ground water due to tidal inflow along the backwater channels. 
Kerala: Salinity of ground water in shallow aquifer has been noticed in 
small pockets in Chellanam and Parur areas of Ernakulam district 
66 

[26 July, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
and Azhikkode area of Trichur district. Salinity in these areas is due to the 
influence of tidal waters. In deeper aquifers, the brackishness in the 
formation water is mainly due to leaching of salts from the aquifer 
materials. 
Maharashtra: instances of salinisation of sub-soil water have been 
reported in localized pockets of co astal districts of Thane, Mumbai, 
Raigarh, Ratnagiri and Sindhudurg. 
Orissa: The extreme southern portion of the coastal sedimentary tract 
indicates a marginal quality of water and the salinity increases towards 
Puri. Southwest of Chilka, quality of formation water is marginal to 
saline with a fresh water zone along the top. In and around Puri, 
brackish water is seen sandwiched between the fresh water zones. Salinity 
problem in these areas is inherent and not due to sea water intrusion. 
Tamil Nadu: Salinisation of ground water due to ingrees of sea water, 
caused by excessive withdrawals of ground water from coastal aquifers has 
been observed in parts of Minjur block, Thiruvallur district and near Kottam, 
Radhapuram block in Tirunelveli district. 
West Bengal: Problem of inland salinity has been observed in parts 
of Haldia area of East Medinipur district. No saline water ingress has been 
noticed in the area. 
Pondicherry: Sea water intrusion in coastal aquifers has been 
reported in parts of Pondicherry region of Union Territory of 
Pondicherry. 
'Water' being a State subject, it is primarily the responsibility of the 
State Governments concerned to take steps to protect sub-soil water. The 
steps taken/proposed to be taken by the State Government concerned/Union 
Government in this regard are as follows:— 
Andhra Pradesh: Under Andhra Pradesh Water, Land & Trees Act, 
2002, construction of new wells has been banned in coastal areas in order 
to prevent upconing of saline ground water from deeper aquifers. No new 
electric connections are given to lift ground water in these areas. Research 
& Development programme on injection of fresh water during floods in 
the river and canals has shown positive results. 
67 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2005] 
Goa: Construction of marginal bunds along the bank of rivers in 
estuarine region to arrest the inundation by saline water during high tide in 
low lying areas and construction of bandharas/barrages across the rivers to 
stop the ingress saline water to deep inland has been undertaken by 
Government of Goa. 
Gujarat: Government of Gujarat had constituted two High Level 
Committees to study the salinity problem of Saurashtra and Kachchh regions 
and to suggest remedial measures thereof. The Committees have 
recommended various remedial measures like construction of tidal 
regulators, bandharas, recharge trenches, recharge wells, recharge 
reservoirs, spreading channels etc. Construction of such works has been 
taken by the Government of Gujarat. 
Karnataka: State Government in coordination with the Zila 
Panchayats is undertaking construction of tidal regulators across the 
rivers and rivulets to avoid saline ingress through the rivers during summer 
months. 
Kerala: State Government is constructing tidal regulators and check 
dams across the backwater channels to prevent movement of tidal waters 
inland. 
Maharashtra: In Kelve Mahim area of Thane district, Sweetwater zone 
area has been demarcated. Sinking of new wells and energisation of pump sets 
on existing wells have been restricted to avoid sea water intrusion due 
to heavy pumping. 
Orissa: Under the Central Sector Scheme of 'Study of Recharge to 
Ground Water' implemented during the IX Plan, construction of tidal 
regulators and desilting of creeks was taken up in Bhadrak, Kendrapara 
and Puri districts of Orissa to arrest saline water intrusion. 
Tamil Nadu: Withdrawal of ground from Minjur well field has been 
stopped. Obtaining a license for sinking of wells and energizing them with 
pump (>1 HP) has been made mandatory in the area falling under 
jurisdiction of Chennai Metropolitan Development Area. Installation of

Discussion with Pakistan on Pipeline Project 
*35.   SHRIMATI AMBIKA SONI: 
DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether he visited Pakistan in the month of May to discuss core issue of 
import of LNG through $4.16 billion Iran-Pakistan-lndia gas pipeline project; 
(b) if so, what is the outcome of discussions held between two countries; 
(c) what other steps were discussed and agreements reached between the two 
countries; 
(d) whether he had also discussions regarding route of pipeline and transit 
fee with Pakistan- and 
(e) if so, whether on this issue also final agreement has been reached? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI MANI 
SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) to (e) The Minister of Petroleum and Natural Gas and 
Panchayati Raj visited Pakistan at the invitation of the Minister for Petroleum 
and Natural Resources of Pakistan, between 5-7 June, 2005. The two Ministers 
reviewed the Iran-Pakistan-India gas pipeline proposal. They agreed that the 
project, which envisages the supply of gas to 
69 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2005] 
Pakistan and India through a transnational pipeline, would go a long way in 
meeting the energy security requiremen ts of the two countries and, thus, 
should be seen as a significant project for the benefit to the people of these 
countries. The Indian and Pakistani delegations agreed to exchange 
information in regard to the financial, technical, commercial, legal and related 
issues to realize a safe and secure world class project. To this end, it was agreed 
that the momentum pertaining to th e project should be accelerated by 
constituting a Joint Working Group (JWG) at Secretary-level, which will meet 
regularly and report progress to the Ministers to facilitate definitive decisions 
by them at the earliest. It was also d ecided that visits at Ministerial-level 
would take place to monitor progress. These and other agreements are 
contained in the Joint Press Statement issued at  the end of the visit of Indian 
Petroleum Minister, a copy of which is placed at Statement-I 
[Refer to the Statement-I appended to the answer to 
S.Q. No. 22 part (a)] 
The first meeting of the India-Pakistan JWG was held in New Delhi on 12-
13 July 2005. Both sides conveyed their serious commitment to address 
various issues pertaining to the proj ect and agreed that once basic issues 
pertaining to the project had been satis factorily resolved between the three 
countries concerned, they would ente r into a "Framework Agreement". The 
two sides also agreed on the crucial importance of urgently appointing their 
respective financial advisory consortia to  advise on the project structure and 
related technical, financial, commercial and legal matters. Details of the 
project such as capital cost, the route of  the pipeline, security issues, transit 
fees etc., will be examined by the countries concerned on the basis of the 
advice provided by the technical consultants. A copy of the Joint Press 
Statement issues at the conclusion of the JWG is placed at Statement-ll.

t*38. DR. PRABHA THAKUR: Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be

prepared any plan by the name of 'River Water Integration Plan'. However, (MOWR) 
(erstwhile Minsitry of Irrigation) and Central Water Commission (CWC)

Reduction of Government's stake in Central PSEs 
*39.  SHRI GIREESH KUMAR SANGHI: 
DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether and ad hoc group of experts on empowerment of Central Public 
Sector Enterprises has recommended that boards of profit-making PSEs be 
allowed to reduce Government stake upto 51 per cent by raising capital from the 
market; 
(b) if so, whetehr expert group has stated that any decision to reduce 
Government's equity to less that 51 per cent in navratnas, miniratnas and public 
sector enterprises with a three years profit making record should be taken only 
with the consent of the Parliament; and 
(c) if so, what are other steps Sengupta's panel has suggested and how its 
recommendations have been accepted? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAME ARAM): (a) The Ad-hoc 
Group of Experts on Empowerment of Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) 
has recommended that the Board of Directors of CPSEs should have the power to 
raise equity capital from the market, so long as the Government's share of the 
overall equity remains above 51 per cent. Further, if raising such equity requires an 
enhancement of the authorised capital, permission for expanding the authorised 
capital should be given in a time bound manner by the Government. At the time of 
granting such approval, the Government may decide to extinguish part of its 
shareholding at the price which the company shares command in the market. 
(b) The Ad-hoc Group of Experts have recommended that in the case of 
Navratnas, Miniratnas and other consistently profit-making CPSEs. (those CPSEs 
which have been making profits for the past three consecutive years and have a 
positive networth) reduction of Government shareholding to less than 51 per cent 
should be taken only with the consent of Parliament, as the ultimate 
representative of the people. 
73 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2005] 
(c) The Ad-hoc Group of Experts have also recommended that the Board of 
Directors of CPSEs should be empowered to divest the shareholding in subsidiary 
companies after complying with SEBI guidelines. However, disinvestment of 
shareholding in such subsidiaries to an extent of more than 50 per cent would 
require the approval of Government. No other recommendations have been 
made with respect to disinvestment of Government shareholding in CPSEs. 
However, since the ambit of the Ad-hoc Group of Experts was wider, a number 
of recommendations have been made with respect to ownership issues and 
powers of CPSEs, audit of Government Companies, Article 12 of the 
Constitution, Parliamentary Accountability and Vigilance Management in 
CPSEs. The recommendations are under examination/consideration.

Tax Exemption on Leasing of Aircrafts 
99. SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: 
SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY: 
Will the Minister of CIVILAVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have made any assesment of the impact of the tax 
exemption on the companies leasing new aircrafts; 
(b) the loss that has to be borne by lA and Al on leasing out its aircrafts to 
others; and 
(c) the total implication of this move in the next five years on lA and Al? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF CIVILAVIATION 
(SHRI PRAFUL PATEL): (a) As per the Union Budget 2005-06 the exemption of tax 
on aircraft lease rental presently available under Sectiion 10(15A) of the Income 
Tax Act has been withdrawn for lease agreements to be entered into on or from 1st 
October 2005 with foreign lessors. The withdrawal of exemption would increase 
the cost of aircraft leasing significantly by 41.82% over and obove the normal ease 
rentals payable by the lessee airlines under fresh lease agreements to be entered 
into on or after 1st October 2005 as per the present corporate tax structure 
applicable to foreign companies. 
(b) and (c) There are no plans of Air India and Indian Airlines to lease 
aircrafts to others.

Expansion of Air Services 
101. PROF. M.M. AGARWAL: Will the Minister of CIVIAL AVIATION be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the number of cities in the country which are not connected by air 
services/helicopter services; 
(b) whether there is any proposal to start new air services to the cities where 
no air services are available; 
(c) if so, the details thereof and by when such new air services would start; 
and 
(d) if not, the specific reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF CIVIL AVIATION 
(SHRI PRAFUL PATEL): (a) to (d) The Government has laid down Route 
Dispersal Guidelines with a view to achieve better regulation of air transport services 
taking into account the need for air transport services of different regions of the 
country including North Eastern region. 
It is however, up to the airlines to provide air services to specific places 
depending upon the traffic demand and commercial viability. As such, the 
airlines are free to operate anywhere in the country subject to compliance of 
Route Dispersal Guidelines issued by the Government. 
The scheduled airlines at present operate to 72 destinations in the country.

148. SHRI B. J. PANDA: Will the the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to

measures to control inflation and borrowings to promote growth; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and

customer friendly? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
S. S. PALANIMANICKAM): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. Containment of inflation 
remains high on the agenda of the government, as inflation hurts everybody, 
particularly the poor whose incomes are not indexed to prices. High inflation 
puts pressure on interest rates leading to a rise in project costs and investment. 
It also tends to reduce real interest rates, thereby adversely affecting the savings 
rate. Anti-inflationary policies of the government include strict fiscal and 
monetary discipline, rationalization of excise and import duties of essential 
commodities so that there is no undue burden on the poor, effective supply-
demand management of essential items through liberal tariff and trade 
policies, and strengthening the public distribution system.

information (b) dissemination of tax payer specific information, (c) 
PAN (Permanent Account Number) and TAN  (Tax Account 
Number) related services, (d) e-filing of returns of income, (e) e-
payment of taxes, (0 processing of retruns/refudns, (g) e-filing of TDS

THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI MANI 
SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) The Committee have recommended policy and structural 
changes and also suggested certain management solutions for improved 
performance of the oil companies in the public sector. Some of the major 
recommendations are: 
1. Merger of Oil Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) may not be 
advisable for the present. 
2. On policy issues there is need for an integrated energy policy setting 
up of Cabinet Committee on Energy headed by the Prime Minister and 
setting up of an Energy Ministry. The Committee has also 
recommended revamping of the existing framework of supervision 
and overview by various surveillance agencies like Central Vigilance 
Commission by setting up of pre-investigation

Board with former PSUs Chiefs, Government and Private Sector 
representatives.

autonomous body with a separate cadre of experts and access to funds. 
4. For overseas ventures, to set up a parallel new entity by Oil India 
Limited. Intense competition in oversea bidding is to be avoided by 
fixing up a limit releated to the production capacity of more than 2 
million tonnes of oil equivalent for OVL, below which the other new 
entity would be permitted to bid. 
5. Another recommendation of the Committee relates to setting up of a 
National Shareholding Trust, modeled after Temasek of Singapore 
and Khazanah of Malaysia, but with a modification. The oil PSUs 
joining the Trust shall continue to retain their PSU character and the 
Trust shall function as non-profit Trust set up under the Societies 
Registration Act or under the companies Act or as a statutory body. The 
Board of the Trust will comprise eminent personalities from Government, 
Public Sector and Private Sector. The Committee expects that the 
greater autonomy to the Trust would ensure synergy in operations.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRI JAY PRAKASH NARAYAN YADAV): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) The "Looming Water Crisis" has been highlighted in the Mid Term

Statement 
Details of "Looming Water Crisis" highlighted in the Mid Term Appraisal 
Document of Tenth Five Year Plan by Planning Commission 
India is already on the verge of a grave water crisis as brought out below. 
* Per capita availability below 1000 m3 is water scarce. 
* This availability is made up of 200 m3 for domestic/industrial use, 200 
m3 for ecology/maintaining minimum flows and 600 m 3 for food 
security. 
* A minimum per capita storage of 1000 m3 is thus required to meet all the 
three uses. 
* Nine river basins with 20 crore population are already under water scarce 
condition. 
* In India, the per capita availability now is 1820 m3 and per capita storage 
is 207 m3. 
* 631 billion cubic metre (BCM) in Ganga-Brahmaputra is 
unutilisable. Hence actual per capita availability is only 1200 m3. 
* Even if all ongoing and potential storages are completed, per capita storage 
will increase only up to 400 m3. 
194 

[26 July, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
* Increasing population will vitiate both per capita availability and per capita 
storage. 
* Improving water use efficiency through proper water management in both irrigated 
and rain fed areas, implementation of watershed programmes and artificial 
recharge of ground water, restoring the traditional water bodies, interlinking of 
rivers, maintaining the water quality standards through pollution abatement 
programmes and downward revision of water supply norms will somewhat 
improve the situation on the water front.

Linking of Rivers 
225. SHRI RK. MAHESHWARI: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether several States are facing heavy floods with the onset of the 
Monsoon this year; 
(b) if so, whether Government are considering to draw special strategy or 
action plan to get rid of the flood problem in the country; and 
(c) whether solution of the flood problem is possible by linking all the rivers 
of the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER-
RESOURCES (SHRI JAY PRAKASH NARAYAN YADAV): (a) Yes Sir. 
(b) Flood throughout the world cannot be fully controlled. It is to be 
managed to the best of ability on technical merit of the problem from place to 
place. However, Flood Management being within the purview of States, the 
schemes for flood control are planned, funded and executed by the 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
201 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2005] 
State Governments. The role of Central Government is technical, catalytical and promotional in 
nature. UFA Government gave special emphasis on this issue in the National Common 
Minimum Programme. 
Central Government, however, has also been initiating various measures for assisting the 
States in the management of floods. The Rashtriya Barh Ayog, set up by the Government of 
India in 1976 to look into flood problem and suggest remedial measures, submitted its 
report in 1980. The recommendations of the Rashtriya BarhAyog which formed the 
framework for flood management strategy in the country were formawred to the various State 
Governments for implementation. Several other expert committees were also constituted 
by the Government from time to time to study the problem relating to flood and its 
management, the recommendations of which were also sent to the respective State 
Governments for implementation. Ganga Flood Control Commission for Ganga Basin 
States constituted in 1972 prepared Comprehensive Plans for Flood Management for all the 23 
river systems of Ganga. Likewise, Brahmaputra Board which started functioning at 
Guwahati in 1982 prepared Master Plans for Flood Management for Brahmaputra, Barak 
and its major tributaries. These plans were forwarded to concerned State Governments for 
implementation. 
During 2004, the Government of India had constituted a Task Force for Flood 
Management/Erosion Control under the Chairmanship of Chairman, Central Water 
Commission with representatives of State Governments, various Central Ministries and 
experts as members to examine the problem of flood and erosion in Assam and 
neighbouring States, West Bengal, Bihar and Eastern Uttar Pradesh. The Task 
Force has inter alia recommended taking up of reservior projects as permanent/long 
term measures flood management. 
The Government of India have been taking effective steps in this direction. An agreement was 
reached with Nepal for survey and investigation and preparation of Detailed Project 
Report for Sapta Koshi High Dam Multipurpose Project and Sun Koshi Storage Cum 
Diversion Scheme for which a Joint Project Office has already been opened in Nepal in 
August, 2004. This project has flood control as one of the major benefits. Nepal has also 
agreed for undertaking the joint feasibility study of Kamla and preliminary study of 
Bagmati Multipurpose Project to ascertain likely constratints in implementation of 
these projects so that the same could be appropriately addressed. 
202 

[26 July, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
As regards North-East, the Master Pl ans prepared by Brahmaputra Board 
have emphasized that the flood problem in the Brahmaputra Valley can be solved 
satisfactorily and enduringly only after construction of large storage dams in the 
basin and that too in the upper part of the basin. Keeping this in view, 
investigations of two most promising project namely the Siang Dihang Dam 
Project and the Subansiri Dam Projects were pursued and project reports were 
prepared by the Brahmaputra Board. These projects which are now to be taken 
up in three stages each have since been transferred to National Hydro-electric Power 
Corporation (NHPC) for detailed investigation and implementation. Detailed 
Project Report for another major project namely Tipaimukh Multipurpose Project on 
river Barak has also been prepared which will inter alia have flood control 
benefits in the Barak Valley. The Government of India also approved 
implementation of Pagladiya Multipurpose of Project in Assam, which has flood 
control as a major benefit. In addition to the above, the Government of India has 
also been providing Central assistance to the State Governments to take up 
critical anti erosion/flood management works. 
(c) Based on various studies conducted, National Water Development Agency 
(NWDA) has identified 30 links for preparing Feasibility Reports (FRs). 
NWDA has completed feasibility reports for 14 links under Peninsular Development 
Component and two links under Himalyan Rivers Development Component. The 
storages envisaged in the interlinking of rivers proposals of NWDA under National 
perspective Plan, by virtue of their capacities and diversion of flood water 
through link canals, will inter-alia provide flood modernisation benefits to 
some extent in the respective basins.

226. SHRI JANARDHAN POOJARY:  Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether a report by the Central Ground Water Board has revealed nitrate 
concentration in excess of the admissible limit in water in various parts of the 
country; 
(b) if so, the details in this regard, State-wise; 
(c) whether consumption of such contaminated water causes cancer or 
damages the nervous system; 
203 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2005] 
(d) if so, the details in this regard; and 
(e) the action initiated to provide safe water in the affected areas, with 
allocation of funds for the purpose? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRI JAY PRAKASH NARAYAN YADAV): (a) and (b) 
Nitrate content in excess of the desirabl e limit of 45 mg/l from ground water 
sources has been reported by Central Ground Water Board (CGWB) in localized 
pockets in various parts of the country. State-wise details of districts parts of 
which are affected by excess nitrate in ground water are given in the Statement 
(See below). 
(c) and (d) As per WHO, the wight of evidence is strongly against a positive 
correlation between nitrate exposures in humans and the risk of cancer. A 
conclusive evidence is yet to be established as regards the relationship 
between nitrite/nitrate and neurological manifestations. 
(e) 'Water' being a State subject, it is primarily the reposibility of the 
concerned State Governments to formulate schems to provide people with 
contamination free water. However, CGWB monitors ground water quality 
periodically to map the changes in it and apprises the State Governments of 
the same taking necessary remedial measures. It has also drilled exploratory 
wells tapping contamination free aquifer zones and has handed over these wells 
to the State Governments, free of cost, for utilisation. 
Department of Drinking Water Supply, under the Ministry of Rural 
Development, is also rendering financial and technicial asistance to the States 
for tackling water quality problems in rural areas through a Centrally Sponsored 
Accelerated Rural Water Supply Programme (ARWSP). 15% of ARWSP funds 
have been exclusively earmarked for Sub Mission projects for tackling water quality 
problems. With effect from 01.04.1998, powers to sanction Sub Mission 
projects have been delegated to States. Funds amounting to Rs. 1899.64 crores, 
Rs. 1646.29 Crores and Rs.2017.88 Crores were released under ARWSP 
(includign normal ARWSP, Desert Development Programme and Natural 
Calamities) by the Department of Drinking Water Supply during the years

Reduction of seats in Andhra Pradesh 
*4. SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRI GIREDDY: Will the Minister of 
HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact the AICTE has reduced 1,220 MCA seats and about 
4,000 Engineering seats in Andhra Pradesh; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(c) the academic year from which the reduction would be operational? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
ARJUN SINGH): (a) to (c) The AII India Council for Technical Education (AICTE) 
reduced a total number of 1370 seats in MCA institutions and 5042 seats in 
Engineering and Technology institutions in the State of Andhra Pradesh for the 
year 2005-06. During the course of a single cpmprehensive inspection of 
institutions, a number of deficiencies including shortage of faculty were 
observed by the AICTE. For the year 2005-06, the Council decided to focus only 
on the most critical deficiency i.e. shortage of faculty. 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
213 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2005] 
Accordingly, the seats were reduced based on the following parameters and 
AICTE norm of faculty to student ratio of 1:15:—  
1. Faculty strengh is 75% or more of required 
strength 
No reduction 
2. Faculty strength is between 50 & 75% Proportionate 
 of required strength reduction 
3. Faculty strength is less than 50% of No admission 
 required strength to a course 
The institutions were given an opportunity to recruit the requisite faculty by 
July 7,2005 so that the seats reduced could be restored. As a result of compliance 
by the institutions, 1105 seats in MCA and 3151 seats in Engineering & 
Technology institutions have since been restored. The reduction in seats 
unless restored would be effective only for the year 2005-06.

1. SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: Will the Minister of URBAN DEVELOPMENT be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that in the last meeting of the National Capital 
Regional Planning Board, development of another new township- 
219 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2005] 
Shahjahanpur, Neemra and Behror in Rajasthan was considered; 
(b) if so, whether the NCR Board have adequate financial resources to provide 
necessary infrastructure facilities to this new township; 
(c) whether NCR is aware that its commitment for provision of Ganga-water 
supply to six Trans-Hindon colonies of Ghaziabad, like Suryanagar, Ramprastha, 
etc. has not been fulfilled due to lack of financial resources; and 
(d) if so, the reasons for not giving priority to the existing commitments 
instead of taking up new liabilities? 
THE MINISTER OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT (SHRI GHULAM NABI 
AZAD): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) A feasibility study has been proposed by the National Capital Region (NCR) 
Planning Board in association with Govt, of Rajasthan to, inter-alia, work out the 
cost of development of the proposed township, generation of resources and 
suggest various models of public, private and joint sector partnership with 
appropriate institutional framework.

for improvement of water supply system in Trans-Hindon area to be 
implemented by the Ghaziabad Nagar Nigam, with an estimated cost of Rs. 
222.68 lakh and loan assistance of Rs. 167.01 lakh. The implementing agency 
has drawn loan amount of Rs. 128.44 lakh and has informed that it will be 
augmenting the water supply in certain  areas of Trans Hindon from their 
resources. 
(d) The NCR Planning Board provides loan assistance to the concerned State 
Governments and their implementing agencies for development of the areas 
falling within the National Capital Region. The NCR Planning Board has 
informed that it has been ab le to meet the commitments for loan assistance as 
and when requested by the State Governments and implementing agencies.

Child Education 
*12. SHRI MATILAL SARKAR: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have any plan to take over the responsibility of education to all 
the children of age group six to fourteen years irrespective of the financial capability of 
their parents; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) if not, the manner in which hundred per cent education would become possible? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
ARJUN SINGH): (a) to (c) Provision of Free and Compulsory Education to children of 
6-14 years is a Constitutional mandate. Under the Centrally sponsored scheme of Sarva 
Shiksha Abhiyan which aims to achieve universal retention at the elementary stage by 
the year 2010, Central Government gives assistance to States, inter alia, for provision of free 
textbooks to all girls and SC/ST boys. Under this scheme, Education Guarantee Scheme 
and Alternative and Innovative Education Centres are also run for children in remote areas 
and those who cannot attend regular schools, and certain other incentives like free uniform 
to girls can also be provided in educationally backward blocks. In addition, Central Assistance 
230 

[26 July, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
is also being given for provision of cooked Mid-Day-Meals to children at the 
Primary stage, and for running residential schools for girls from weaker sections in 
selected educationally backward blocks. Taken together, these measures 
substantially address the problem of participation of children belonging to 
poor families in elementary education.

SHRI JANARDAN DWIVEDI.

Ban on showing of film 
*20. SHRI RAM JETHMALANI: 
SHRI RAJ MOHINDER SINGH MAJITHA: 
Will the Minister of INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that after a strong protest the show of "Jo Bole So Nihal" film 
had been stopped in a number of States; 
(b) if so, the names of such States; and 
(c) the reasons for not imposing a ban on showing of this film anticipating a strong 
protest thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING (SHRI S JAIPAL 
REDDY): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Though the Central Board of Film Certification (CBFC) does not maintain such 
information, they have informally ascertained that the film was taken off the screen by the 
distributors in the States of Punjab, Haryana and Himachal Pradesh on 20.05.2005. After 
bomb blasts in two theatres in Delhi on 22.05.05, the distributors took off the movie from 
theatres in the States of Delhi, Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal, Assam, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu 
and parts of Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan on 23.05.05. 
(c) The film was viewed by a duly constituted Examination Committee and 
subsequently on the directions of the Punjab and Haryana High Court by a Reviewing 
Committee. Both the Committees cleared the film for public exhibition with a 'UA' certificate. 
Further, the Director and Producer of the film informed the Court that they had approached 
the highest Sikh Body, namely, Akal Takht Sahibji, Amritsar, who had constituted a 
Committee of six members to view the film on 8th May, 2005. The Committee had not 
found anything in the movie offending the religious feelings of the Sikhs. In fact, the only 
recommendation made by the Committee was that it should be clarified in the advertisement 
of the film that it is not a religious movie. This clarification was incorporated by the 
producer. 
Moreover, as per the Cinematograph Act, 1952, once a film is certified by the Central 
Board of Film Certification (CBFC) it has no powers to stop

[26 July, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
the screening of the film. The revisionary powers of the Central Government under 
Section 6 of the Cinematograph Act, 1952 were struck down by the Supreme 
Court in their judgement in the Shankarappa Vs. Union of India case in 2000. 
Therefore, the Central Government does not have any power to intervene or 
review the decision of the CBFC.

1. SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA: Will the Minister of CULTURE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Comptroller and Auditor General of India has in his Audit 
Report ending the 31st March, 2004 (no. 4 of 2005) has adversely commented 
on the lack of any proper standard or norms for acquiring, collecting and 
preserving art objects in the Indian Museum, Victoria Memorial and Asiatic 
Society in Kolkata; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and Government's reaction thereto; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that security system in these institutions is 
inadequate and leaves much to be desired; and 
(d) if so, the steps proposed to be taken to address these shortcomings? 
THE MINISTER OF CULTURE (SHRI S. JAIPAL REDDY): (a) and (b) 
Yes, Sir. In Chapter III of C&AG Report No. 4 of 2005 (Civil) for Indian 
Museum, Asiatic Society and Victoria  Memorial Hall, Kolkata the Audit 
commented on the absence of standards or norms in the four functional areas of 
acquisition, documentation, preservation/conservation and safe custody of 
artifacts. 
The Indian Museum, Asiatic Society and Victoria Memorial Hall do follow 
standards norms for acquisition, documentation and conservation/ preservation 
and safe custody of artifacts. These institutions maintain methodical and 
scientific standards which are based on the specific needs of the institutions. 
However, observations made in the Audit Report have been noted for further 
improvement. 
(c) The Audit Report also commented on inadequacy of security systems in 
these institutions. 
(d) According to the recommendations of the Central Advisory Board of 
243 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2005] 
Museums and the Ministry of Culture, a three-tier security system has been 
introduced in the Indian Museum. The Ministry of Culture has constituted a 
Committee under the chairman ship of Director General, National Museum for 
assessment of security requirement of its museums. The Committee has also 
assessed the security requirement of I ndian Museum, Kolkata, and has made 
certain recommendations. Ministry of Culture has issued directions to Indian 
Museum to implement the recommendation of the Committee. The master plan of 
the Victoria Memorial Hall galleries and stores has included the crucial aspects of 
security and surveillance and Central Industrial Security Force (CISF) 
authorities, engaged to study an effective security system. In Asiatic Society, 
the recommendations relating to increase in the number of cameras for close-
circuit TV and modifications/renovation work of the main gate were accepted.

Buddhist votive stupas from excavations at Udaygiri, Distt. Jajpur, Orissa,

stupas of varying dimensions, made of bricks and stones. These stupas were 
constructed on squarish, rectangular or circular platforms. The bases of some 
stupas have circular depressions for keeping terracotta sealings bearing Buddhist

variously to circa 1st—-12th century AD. Besides, a votive stupa has been

datable to circa 9th-10th century AD.

DWIVEDI: 
SHRI MOTILAL VORA: 
SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA: 
Will the Minister of CULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the structure of Konark Temple and its magnificent celestial 
chariot and ..tone sculpture is fast turning into a colossal ruin; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that 25 per cent of its sculptural embellishment etched 
on inert stones, have been defaced by erosion and lost forever; 
(c) if so, the details thereof and the reasons for neglecting maintenance of the 
temple; and 
245 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2005] 
(d) the steps proposed to be taken to preserve the heritage of this temple? 
THE MINISTER OF CULTURE (SHRI S. JAIPAL REDDY): (a) No, Sir. 
(b) to (d) The architectural members of the temple built of Khondolite, a soft stone, is 
subject to constant wind action as the temple is located close to the sea. The salt laden 
sea wind causes surface damage to the stone members. This also causes crystallization of 
soluble salts leading to weathering and corrosion of the stone members. 
Following remedial measures are adopted regularly to control weathering of stone 
members and to conserve the heritage. 
(i) Soluble salts are removed by repeated paper pulp treatment. 
(ii) Micro-vegetational and fungicidal growth are being treated chemically. 
(iii) The weathering effects are minimized through stone consolidation. 
(iv) Water tightening and underpinning of the structure are carried out using 
traditional mortar. 
(v) Missing stone members of the adhishtana were restored using the original stone 
members found scattered in the temple complex or with new stones, if 
necessary.

(a) whether the Private National Curriculum Framework, 2005 seeks to draw 
out creativity, eliminate airtight compartmentalization of subject, make education 
more relevant and provide" avenues for greater participation of Panchayati Raj 
institutions and civil society groups in making it a tool for social change; 
(b) if so, whether there is a renewed attempt also to implement three

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALI ASHRAF FATMI): (a) The NCERT has 
been assigned a special role for preparing and promoting a National 
Curriculum Framework (NCF). The National Policy on Education, 1986 
mandates a five yearly review of the various parameters of the Policy. 
Accordingly, consequent on a decision, the process of the review of the NCF 
was initiated by the NCERT through wide ranging consultations and 
deliberations across the country. 
The draft NCF 2005 si nce prepared includes the following salient 
features:— 
(i) It is based on the following four guiding principles:— 
Connecting knowledge of life outside the school, 
Ensuring that learning shifts away from rote methods, 
Enriching the curriculum so that it goes beyond textbooks, 
Making examinations more flexible. 
(ii) The NCF also focuses on the child  as an active learner, thus giving 
primacy to the children's experiences, their voices and their 
participation. It views children as active participants in the 
construction of knowledge, and states that schools should recognize 
the innate ability and creativity of each child to construct his/her own 
knowledge. 
(iii) It recommends the softening of subject boundaries so that children can 
get a taste of integrated knowledge and joy of understanding. 
(iv) It reaffirms faith in panchayati raj institutions to enable people to 
think, decide and act in their coll ective interest, to provide greater 
participation of people in development. 
(b) The NCF 2005 makes a renewed attempt to implement the Three 
Language Formula, emphasizing mother tongue as a medium of instruction 
including tribal languages. 
(c) and (d) The draft NCF 2005 was discussed in the meeting of the 
Central Advisory Board of Education (CABE) held on the 7th June, 2005

Fear Psychosis due to examination 
33. SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the numb er of students suffering from traumatic 
disaster relating to fear of examinations is on the rise; 
281 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2005] 
(b) whether it is also a fact that the exam-related stress is, sometimes leading 
to suicides; 
(c) if so, the steps Government propose to take in this regard; 
(d) whether it is a fact that a meeting of experts was held; and 
(e) if so, what are the suggestions/recommendations made by the experts? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALIASHRAF FATMI): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. 
The problem of increasing stress among students during examinations and 
instances of some students committing suicide due to failure in examination 
and stress have been engaging the attention of the Government. However, 
there are various contributory factors such as competition, peer & parental 
pressure, fast changing socio and economic conditions, lack of employment 
opportunities and fear of failure in examinations which could become the 
cause of tragedies like suicides among students. 
The Ministry is deeply concerned with the issue of higher stress level among 
students caused by the public examinations at the end of class X and XII 
conducted by various boards, Joint Entrance Examination for NTs and other 
entrance examinations. 
(c) to (e) To address the question of promoting equality in access to 
education as also allow the students to have a stress free environment of joyful 
learning, the Ministry had convened a meeting with Eminent Educationists, 
Principals, representatives from premier Institutions such as the Indian 
Institutes of Technology and Indian Institutes of Management, Heads of the 
Boards of Examination and others on 24th March, 2005. It was unanimously 
agreed that there must by systemic reforms to eliminate exam related stress. The 
issue was further discussed in the conference of Council of Boards of Secondary 
Education (COBSE) held on 1st May, 2005, the CBSE has since taken the 
following steps: 
(i) Segregating the syllabus: 
The Board has segregated the syllabus for classes IX & X and also for 
classes XI & XII. The examinations for classes IX & XI based on the 
prescribed syllabus will be conducted by the schools concerned 
282 

[26 July, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
while for classes X & XII, public ex aminations are being conducted by 
the Board. 
(ii) Single theory paper for all subjects: 
The Board has provision for only one theory paper for all subjects in the 
public examinations for classes X & XII. However, other State Boards 
were also requested to have once question paper for each subject in the 
public examinations. 
(iii) Extra time for examination: 
The Board has taken a decision in the recent Governing Body meeting that the 
studetns be allowed an extra 15 minutes time before the commencement 
of the examinations to study the question papers. It is also been decided 
that the question papers will be set in such a way that they can be 
answered in a time period of two and a half hours while the students 
will have a time period of three hours for completion of the question 
paper. 
(iv) Grading pattern: 
The Board has initiated necessary steps for finalizing the pattern of grades 
which would be introduced at the earliest. 
(v) Flexibility in the choice of subjects: 
Presently, the Board offers adequate flexibility in the choice of subjects 
at the senior school level in order to meet the requirements multiple 
intelligence of the students. However, at the secondary level, the Board is 
implementating the National Core Curriculum with a prescribed set of 
subjects.

Universalization of Computer Literacy 
36. SHRI R. P. GOENKA: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
287 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2005] 
(a) whether it is a fact that recently a new initiative has been taken to launch 
the "Information and Communication Technology in Schools Scheme" aimed 
at universalization of the computer literacy percolating down to the students in 
small towans and mufussil India; 
(b) if so, the details thereof, indicating the funds earmarked for the 
purpose, modalities formalized for its implementation and its present status; and 
(c) the extent to which the new scheme is an improvement on the existing 
two schemes nick-named "CLASS" and "revised-CLASS" and would enable 
the students to acquire necessary skills needed for both the higher education and 
gainful employment? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALIASHRAF FATMI): (a) to (c) Yes sir, this 
Department has launched a new scheme viz 'Information and Communication 
Technology (ICT) @ Schools' by merging the Educational Technology (ET) 
Scheme and the revised Computer Literacy and Studies in Schools (CLASS) 
Scheme during 2004-05. Universalization of Computer Literacy is one of the 
components of the scheme. 
Under the ICT @ Schools scheme funds are provided to States/UTs for 
imparting computer education in Government & Government aided 
Secondary and Senior Secondary Schools on the basis of fixed ratio of 75:25 
for General States and 90:10 for Special Category States including NER states. 
The scheme also provides for contribution of 25% of funds from the MPLAD 
scheme in addition or as an alternative to State Governments' contribution. 
The ICT @ Schools scheme is the improved version of the revised CLASS 
scheme and the ET scheme, wherein one of the components relates to State 
Institutes of Educational Technology. Under the revised scheme Rs. 20,000/- is 
released for each neighbourhood school under the Universalization of Computer 
Literacy component, which was Rs. 15,000/-per school under the revised CLASS 
scheme. The new ICT @ Schools Scheme is different from the revised CLASS 
Scheme in the sense that it has more items of expenditure, States/UTs are free to 
integrate the scheme with similar State programmes, Project Monitoring and 
Evaluation Group (PM & EG) is empowered to effect modification depended upon 
changes in 
288 

[26 July, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Technological environment and financial norms, greater outlay for 
educational software, internet, teacher training, stationery etc. 
Block grant Scheme for IITs/IIMs 
37. SHRI R. P. GOENKA: 
SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY: 
SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: 
Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that recently a proposal has been formulated to replace 
the hitherto prevalent formula-linked grants to certain institutes of higher 
learning, like the NTs, IIMs etc. by a modified block grant scheme, with a view 
to ensuring their greater financial and functional autonomy; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the present status of its implementation; 
(c) the details of any fresh guidelines laid down for a review of the pattern 
of funding; and 
(d) whether any stipulation has been put, say if the corpus reached to a certain 
level, the scheme would be withdrawn from that particular IIT or IIM? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALIASHRAF FATMI): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) The Scheme of Block Grant (Non-Plan Grant) now being 
introduced will remain operative for a period of five years from 2005-2006 to 2009-
2010 in respect of the followig Centrally funded Institutes:— 
(i)  India Institutes of Technology at Bombay, Delhi, Kanpur, Kharagpur, 
Madras, Guwahati, Roorkee; 
(ii)  Indian Institutes of Management at Ahmedabad, Bangalore, Kolkata, 
Lucknow, Indore and Kozhikode; 
(iii)  Indian Institute of Science, Bangalore; 
(iv) Indian School of Mines, Dhanbad; 
(v)  National Institute of Industrial Engineering (NITIE), Mumbai; 
289 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2005] 
(vi)  National Institutes of Technical Teachers Training & Research (NITTTR) at 
Bhopal, Chandigarh, Chennai and Kolkata; 
(vii) School of Planning and Architecture, New Delhi. 
The base year for determining annual grant-in-aid under Non-Plan in respect of the 
above institutes from 2005-06 to 2009-10 shall be 2004-2005. The grant-in-aid 
sanctioned to these Institutes in the year 2004-2005 shall be inclusive of unspent 
balance adjusted/permitted to be carried forward for utilization during 2004-2005, 
These Institutes shall be allowed to retain the internal Revenue/Income generated by 
them and their entitlement for annual grant-in-aid during the Block Grant period shall not 
be adjusted against any increase in income. Special grants shall be provided as "force 
majeure" in the event of revision of scales of pay and other unforeseen events. The 
force majeure clause will, however, not be invoked for any increase in rate of 
Dearness Allowance/Dearness Relief payable to employees/pensioners of the 
Institutes. 
(d) The Government would provide matching grant equivalent to the annual 
savings from the regular non-plan gran t and other receipts including internal 
revenue and earnings from consultancy, entrance examination like JEE, CAT etc. 
and other continuing education programmes but, excluding receipts earmarked for 
designated purposes in accordance with the terms & conditions of such donations with 
due approval of the Finance Committee & Board of Governors. The matching grant would 
be available till the Endowment Fund has reached the level of Rs. 100 Crores for each 
Institute in respect of IITs/IISc and Rs. 50 crore in respect of IIMs and other Institutes. 
Matching grant equivalent to the total savings transferred to the Endowment Fund in a 
financial Year shall be sanctioned to the Institute in the following financial year. 
Institute having funds in excess of the ceiling as prescribed above may utilize the same for 
infrastructural development. The proceeds from the Endowment Fund by way of interests 
earned annually would be available to the Institutes for supplementing the plan grant 
being given by the Government and if required, for meeting essential operational 
expenses. There is no proposal at present to withdraw the Scheme on reaching the 
limits prescribed for purpose of sanctioning matching grants.

Piracy in film industry 
53. SHRIMATI SUKHBUNS KAUR: Will the Minister of INFORMATION 
AND BROADCASTING be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the film Industry has suffered heavy losses due to 
the prevalent menance of unchecked piracy; and 
317 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2005] 
(b) the steps taken and being taken to check piracy effectively? 
THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING (SHRI S. 
JAIPAL REDDY): (a) According to the Federation of Indian Chamber of Commerce 
and Industry (FICCI) the revenue loss from film piracy is about Rs. 1200 Crores annually. 
As far as the Music Industry is concerned, the Indian Music Industry (IMI) has informed 
that the size of the music industry has fallen from Rs. 1000 Crores in 1999 to Rs. 500 
Crores in 2004 due to piracy. The Ministry does not have any other data. 
(b) The Copyright Act, 1957, which fails under the purview of the Ministry of Human 
Resource Development contains, inter alia, legal provisions regarding copyright in 
cinematograph films and music. The responsibility for dealing with offences under the 
Copyright Act rests with the police authorities of the State Governments and Union 
Territory Administrations. Copyright Enforcement cells have been set up in most 
States/UT Administrations headed by a senior police officer to deal with such 
offences. 
Apart from this, the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting has taken the following 
steps to fight piracy in the film sector: 
• This Ministry has a Plan Scheme to undertake activities relating to anti piracy 
measures. 
• The Ministry has initiated action to formulate appropriate training modules for 
police officers to train them for anti-piracy. 
• In September 2001, Ministry of l&B brought together representatives of the film 
producers, multi-service operators and cable operators who have jointly resolved 
not to exhibit films without valid permission from the copyright holders. 
• Recognizing that high levels of entertainment tax lead to piracy, the Committee for 
Development of the Entertainment Sector, a sub committee of the 24th State 
Information Ministers' Conference, recommended that the rate of entertainment 
tax be lowered to a ceiling of 45%. In the recent SIMCON it was felt that the 
ceiling should be further lowered to 25-30%. 
• The same Committee also recommended appointment of senior police 
318 

[26 July, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
officers in States to work in co-ordination with the entertainment 
industry, as nodal officers. 
• During the Budget of 2003-04, audio CDs were exempted from excise duty to 
do away with the price advantage available to pirated CDs. 
• The Public Service Broadcasting Trust has been entrusted with the task of 
making a film on piracy. 
• The Cable Television Networks Regulation Act has been amended in 2000, to 
prohibit a Cable operator from transmitting or re-transmitting any 
programme or channel for which the Copyright holder has not granted 
him a license. 
• The Ministry has requested Chief Secretaries of all States to advise District 
Magistrates and Superintendents of Police to include anti piracy 
measures in their monthly activity reports. 
• In the meeting of the 25th State Information Ministers, piracy emerged as a 
key concern for most State Governments and some measures were 
considered in order to deter piracy in the film and music industry. 
• This Ministry has also made suggestions for restricting incidence of piracy 
in the film and music sector while considering the on going amendments 
to the Copyright Act. 
• National Film Development Corporation Ltd. has been commissioned to 
make spots for running an anti piracy campaign on prominent national 
and satellite channels. This Ministry has requested industry Associations to 
persuade films stars to work on this campaign in order to make it an 
effective one. 
• This Ministry is consulting FICCI to explore the possibility of enacting an 
Optical Disc Law.

(b) Recognition of a political party as National Party is governed by the 
provisions of paragraph 6B of the Election Symbols (Reservation and 
Allotment) Order, 1968. Recognition is based on the poll performance of 
political parties at General Election to the House of the People and Legislative 
Assemblies. For recognition as National Party, a political party should satisfy any 
of the following conditions on the basis of general election(s):— 
(i) The candidates set up the party, in any four or more States, at the last 
general election to the House of the People, or to the Legislative Assembly 
of the State concerned, have secured not less than six percent of the total 
valid votes polled in each of those States at that general election; and, in 
addition, it has returned at least four members to the House of the 
People at the aforesaid last general election from any State or States; or 
(ii) At the last general election to the House of the People, the party has 
won at least two percent of the total number of seats in the House of the 
People, any fraction exceeding half being counted as one; and the party's 
candidates have been elected to the House from not less than three 
seats; or 
(iii) The party is recognized as State Party in at least four States.

by various political parties at the general election(s) concerned.

State parties in different States. For recognition as State party, a political 
party should satisfy any of the following conditions on the basis of general 
election in the State concerned:— 
(i) At the last general election to the Legislative Assembly of the State, the 
candidates set up by the party have secured not less than six percent of 
the total valid voted polled in the State; and, in addition, the party has 
returned at least two members to the Legislative Assembly of that State 
at such general election; or 
(ii) At the last general election to the House of the People from that State,

the total valid votes polled in the State; and, in addition, the party has 
returned at least one member to the House of the People from that State 
at such general election; or

party has won at least three percent of the total number of seats in the 
Legislative Assembly, (any fraction exceeding half being counted as one), or at 
least three seats in the Assembly, whichever is more; or 
(iv) At the last general election to the House of the People from the State,

Forest rights for ST 
82. SHRI C. RAMCHANDRAIAH: 
SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA: 
Will the Minister of TRIBAL AFFAIRS be pleased to state; 
(a) whether it is proposed to pass a legislation with regard to recognition of 
forest rights for the Scheduled Tribes; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether the Bill is likely to be introduced during the current Monsoon 
Session of Parliament; and 
(d) if so, the steps taken so far in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF TRIBAL AFFAIRS (SHRI PR. KYNDIAH): (a) to (d) 
Yes, Sir. The Ministry of Tribal Affa irs has been mandated to formulate a 
comprehensive Central Legislation to redress the historical injustice done to forest 
dwelling Scheduled Tribes by providing for clear assertion of their 
354 

[26 July, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
legal rights on land and other traditional forest rights. This Ministry has 
prepared a draft "The Scheduled Tribes (Recognition of Forest Rights) Bill, 2005," 
to provide a legislative frame for recognition of the aforementioned rights, in 
consultation with the concerned Ministries, including the Ministry of Law & 
Justice. 
The proposed Bill seeks to recognize such rights on land, minor forest 
produce, etc. for bona fide livelihood needs of the forest dwelling Scheduled Tribes. 
The Bill was posted on the website of the Ministry seeking comments of the 
public and all stakeholdes till 10.7.05. The proposed Bill is still a tentative draft 
Bill and to be finalized as per the established procedure taking views and 
comments received from the stakeholders into consideration. No time frame 
can be indicated at this stage.

be pleased to state:

provides right to land to the forest dwelling Scheduled Tribes under certain 
conditions; 
(b) if so, the details thereof;

comprehensive Central Legislation to redress the historical injustice done to forest

land and other traditional forest rights. This Ministry has prepared a draft "The

Water crisis in Delhi 
85. SHRI B.J. PANDA: 
SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: 
Will the Minister of URBAN DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that there is an acute shortage of 
drinking water in the capital city Delh i as there is a big gap between demand 
and supply; 
(b) the measures proposed by Government to optimize the capacity to meet 
the shortfall; and 
(c) the short term and long term measures proposed to be taken to address 
the chronic water shortage problem of Delhi? 
THE MINISTER OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT (SHRI GHULAM NABI 
AZAD): (a) to (c) The Delhi Jal Board (DJB) has informed that against the total 
requirement of 850 million gallons per day (mgd) of water in Delhi, it is 
supplying, on an average, 675 mgd of water in Delhi for a population of about 
140 lakhs. This works out to about 210 Itrs. per capita per day.

constructed water treatment plants at Sonia Vihar and Nangloi with a total 
capacity of 180 mgd. In addition water treatment plants at Dwarka, Bavana and 
Okhla with a total capacity of 80 mgd have also been planned, DJB has also taken 
action to reduce the seepage losses and recycling of waste water at existing water 
treatment plants with a view to further add to the availability of water in Delhi.

t97. SHRI NAND KISHORE YADAV. Will the Minister of URBAN 
EMPLOYMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that no target has been fixed under the National Slum 
Development Programme; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(c) the details of the data on the basis of which problem of slums is solved; and 
(d) Government's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
EMPLOYMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (KUMARI SELJA): (a) and 
(b) As per the provisions of National Slum Development Programme (NSDP), the 
implementation of the programme is with the State Governments. Hence, the State 
Governments formulate specific plans, programmes and schemes for development of 
slums in various towns/ cities as per their priorities and made necessary provisions 
therefor, in their respective State plans. 
(c) Since the inception of NSDP, each year the Planning Commission allocates the 
State-wise funds on the pro-rata basis of slum population of States/UTs, keeping a 
minimum amount reserved for smaller States. 
(d) With a view to ameliorate the living conditions of slum dwellers a programme 
known as National Slum Development Programme (NSDP) was launched at national 
level by the Government in 1996 for the development of urban slums. 
Beside, a centrally sopnsored schemes called Valmiki Ambedkar Awas Yojana 
(VAMBAY) was launched on 2.12.2001 with a view to ameliorate the conditions of the 
urban slum dwellers living below the poverty line who do not possess adequate shelter. The 
Scheme has the primary objective to facilitate adequate construction and upgradation of 
the dwelling units for the slum dwellers and to provide health and enabiling urban environment 
through community toilets under Nirmal Bharat Abhiyan, a component of the Scheme.

SHRI KARNENDU BHATTACHARJEE (Assam): Mr. Deputy 
Chairman, Sir, I rise to speak about the flood situation in the country. I have 
just heard my colleague, the hon. MP from Gujarat, who explained everything 
about Gujarat. In the meantime, Central Government has taken all steps in 
Himachal Pradesh, Gujarat, Maharash tra, Bihar and other places in the 
country. I am residing in such a place  where there are always floods. Last 
year, there was a tremendous flood in Assam. This was the most devastating 
flood in the history' of Assam in which twelve million people were displaced, 
large sectors of crops were damaged and road link of the North-East with the 
rest of India was totally cut off. But our hon. Prime Minister visited this site, 
and the UPA Chairman, hon. Soniaji, also visited this site.   They have 
instituted a Task Force.   The Minister in charge

of Flood Control is not here. But as a Ruling Party Member, I must say that 
though you have instituted this Task Force, but it is not yet implemented. Sir, 
I am observing one thing that in 1981, the Brahmaputra Board was instituted, 
but no concrete action has yet been taken in that regard. We had raised this 
issue at the time of NDA Government an d I have already brought this to the 
notice of our Government as well, but  there is no action. There is no 
permanent Chairman. It is like a White Elephant. I am saying it is nothing but 
a White Elephant. The Prime Minister has also got convinced about this and 
accordingly he formed this Task Force, but it is not yet implemented. J do not 
know what is the position at present. 
Sir, on 21 st July, 2005, there was another spate of floods in Assam in

permanent solution to save Assam from the losses of lives, crops and

solution. Big promises from the Centre do come. The Centre has committed 
some money. I appreciate that our hon. Prime Minister has taken such steps.

Minister is here. I heard Shri Priyaranjan Dasmunsi, the Minister of Water

the Minister of Water Resources to take care about the flood situation not

south Bengal, north

SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, I want to take

monitors the monsoon on day-to-day basis - while the all-India picture is

particularly and whether, in fact, he expects some impact on oilseeds and

Sir, my second question is on the monsoon itself. And I am glad that 
the distinguished scientist, Dr. Kasturir angan, is present here because one of 
the points that I do want to raise concerns the institute to which he belongs, 
the Indian Institute of Science. Sir, it is a fact that in the last few years, the 
track record of monsoon prediction in this country, the track record of 
predicting whether this region is going to have floods or that region is going to 
have drought has come under severe stress and questioning. We know for a 
fact that the drought of 2002 was not predicted; the good performance of the 
monsoon in 2003 was not predicted; the monsoon shortfall in 2004 was not 
predicted; and experts have said that even the monsoon performance of this 
year in terms of prediction leaves a lot to be desired. Sir, last month, in a 
scientific magazine called 'Current Science', which is brought out by the 
Indian Institute of Science, Bangalore, there is an authoritative article called 
'Monsoon Prediction: Why Yet Another Failure' by three scientists, who are 
considered to be the best we have in this business, Sulochana Gadgil, M. 
Rajeevan and Ravi Nanijundiah. Sir, it is a very detailed analysis of the 
performance of the Indian Meteorological Department in predicting the 
performance of the monsoon and thereby the existence of floods and droughts. 
Sir, I just want to quote the last concluding paragraph of this analysis. This 
says, "Our analysis of the predictions generated by the empirical models used 
operationally by the Indian Meteorological Department since 1932..." Sir, this 
is very important, "Our analysis of the predictions generated by the empirical 
models used operationally by the Indian Meteorological Department since 
1932 suggests that the performance of these models based on the relationship 
of the monsoon rainfall to atmospheri c or oceanic conditions over different 
parts of the globe has not been satisfactory." Sir, there is a worse indictment to 
follow. It goes on to say, "They have not been improved over eight decades, 
despite several changes in the operational models and better understanding of 
monsoon variability." Sir, the scientific conclusion is that all the models that 
we are using today are highly unsatisfactory, do not lead to any reliable or 
robust predictions of the monsoon and, therefore, we are not in a position to 
assess which regions are going to be prone to floods and which regions are 
going to be prone to droughts in a particular monsoon situation. So, Sir, my 
request to the hon. Minister is that since he really is the nodal point to review 
the monsoon performance and he gets the data on a day-to-day basis from the 
National Centre for Medium Range W eather Forecasting, whether he would 
be in a position to take a leadership role and -bring about a very substantial 
upgradation in the technical capacity, in the

sections of our population. So, my second request to the Minister would be to
